claims.text: Five-or-more-metal near-equiatomic nanoparticles can initially crystallize as a single solid-solution phase.
High local compositional disorder is the key determinant of stability from 473 to 1923 K.
High local compositional disorder suppresses elemental diffusion.
Suppressed elemental diffusion delays phase decomposition over a wide temperature range.
The nanoparticles will be subjected to repeated isothermal heating cycles over 473–1923 K.
In-situ high-temperature electron microscopy and XRD under controlled application-relevant environments can be used to evaluate stability.
High configurational entropy is associated with sluggish diffusion in these nanoparticles.
Sluggish diffusion hinders atomic rearrangement and elemental segregation.
Multi-element synergy in near-equiatomic compositions generates large atomic-scale disorder.
Atomic-scale disorder lowers the thermodynamic driving force for phase segregation.
A reduced driving force for segregation helps preserve a single-phase structure over a broad temperature window.
Five-plus-metal near-equiatomic nanoparticles will be more thermally stable than matched ternary or quaternary nanoparticles.
Five-plus-metal nanoparticles will show minimal phase separation after prolonged high-temperature exposure.
Five-plus-metal nanoparticles will show minimal morphological change after prolonged high-temperature exposure.
Lower-entropy control compositions will show decomposition, phase changes, and microstructural segregation under identical conditions.
Excessively long exposure above approximately 1600 K can overcome the proposed stabilization and cause partial demixing.
Strongly segregating impurities can overcome diffusion barriers and induce partial demixing.
Extended-duration in-situ data above 1600 K are sparse, leaving the upper time-temperature stability limit uncertain.
Comparable phase separation or compositional inhomogeneity in the five-metal samples and lower-element controls would falsify the claimed stability enhancement.
